## Introduction: Rising Diagnosis
- Cystic neoplasms of the pancreas are now a well-defined radiographic entity
- Increased use of cross-sectional imaging, better imaging quality, and aging population
- Diagnosis rate: estimated 2.6 cystic lesions per 100 individuals per year
- Detection by modality:
  - Abdominal ultrasonography: 0.21%
  - Computed tomography: 2.6%
  - MRI/MRCP: 2.4% to 49.1%
  - Autopsy studies: up to 50%

## Classification of Pancreatic Cysts
- WHO classification: neoplastic vs nonneoplastic
- Neoplastic cysts: intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, mucinous cystic neoplasms, serous cystadenomas, solid pseudopapillary neoplasms
- Nonneoplastic cysts: pseudocysts
- Neoplastic cysts further categorized:
  - Mucin-producing: IPMNs, MCNs
  - Nonmucin-producing: SCAs, SPTs
- Mucinous cysts are malignant precursor lesions, lined by endoderm-derived columnar epithelium
- Nonmucinous cysts are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium

## Diagnostic Challenge and Management Shift
- Ability to differentiate neoplastic pancreatic cystic neoplasms without resection continues to evolve
- Serous cysts often differentiated from mucinous cysts by cross-sectional imaging and EUS with cyst fluid analysis
- Next-generation sequencing of pancreatic cyst fluid helps distinguish cyst types and predict invasive carcinoma risk
- Cystic lesions remain a diagnostic challenge
- Increasing incidence and differential diagnosis
- Management has changed to selective resection based on clinicopathologic variables and natural history

## Clinicopathologic Variables: Pseudocysts
- Majority of patients with pancreatic cysts have nonneoplastic inflammatory pseudocysts
- Develop as a complication of acute pancreatitis
- Pseudocyst: fluid collection devoid of an epithelial lining
- Reported in as many as 50% of patients who experience acute pancreatitis
- Up to 20% of unexplained pancreatitis occurs because of cystic neoplasms
- Consider cystic neoplasm in differential diagnosis of incidental cyst associated with pancreatitis
- Pseudocysts managed with observation, endoscopic drainage, or operative drainage

## Clinicopathologic Variables: Cystic Neoplasms
- Cystic neoplasms make up approximately 10% to 15% of cystic lesions of the pancreas
- Heterogeneous group ranging from benign to malignant
- Cystic lesions with risk of invasive carcinoma: IPMNs and MCNs
- SPTs and SCAs have very low risk for invasive carcinoma
- Other benign cystic lesions: lymphoepithelial cysts, simple cysts, mucinous nonneoplastic cysts
- Most common cystic neoplasms encountered by surgeons: IPMNs, MCNs, SCAs
- Massachusetts General Hospital study of 851 resected pancreatic cystic neoplasms: these three lesions made up 77% of all lesions

## Table 60.1: Abbreviations
- BD: branch duct
- CEA: carcinoembryonic antigen
- HGD: high-grade dysplasia
- IPMN: intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm
- MCN: mucinous cystic neoplasm
- MD: main duct
- MPD: main pancreatic duct
- SCA: serous cystadenoma
- SPT: solid pseudopapillary tumor

## Serous Cystadenomas: Background
- First characterized by Compagno and Oertel in 1978 as microcystic and glycogen-rich
- Seminal distinction of SCAs from mucinous cysts such as MCNs and IPMNs
- Around half of patients with SCAs are found incidentally
- Symptoms: abdominal pain, palpable mass, weight loss
- Symptoms usually related to mass effect
- Jaundice due to bile duct compression is infrequent
- SCAs can be associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease
- Reported in 2.7% to 9.5% of patients with VHL
- VHL-associated SCAs: diagnosed at younger age around 25 years; benign course

## SCA: Morphology and Imaging
- Morphologic varieties: microcystic, macrocystic or oligocystic, mixed microcystic/macrocystic, and solid SCA
- Grossly: septations, thick fibrous walls, innumerable small cysts containing clear thin fluid
- Microcystic SCAs often have classic honeycomb appearance
- May have calcified central scar with or without hemorrhage
- Septa may centrally coalesce into characteristic stellate scar
- Stellate scar with or without calcification is pathognomonic for SCA
- Oligocystic appearance: single large cyst; difficult to distinguish from mucinous lesions
- Solid component often visualized due to fibrous nature; if other SCA features present, not concerning for invasive carcinoma

## SCA: Malignant Potential
- SCAs generally considered benign lesions
- Serous cystadenocarcinoma is extremely uncommon; about 30 cases reported
- Many reported malignant SCAs were locally invasive
- Only 14 of 30 cases 46.6% had evidence of metastasis
- Despite metastasis, long-term prognosis was excellent
- True incidence of invasive carcinoma within SCAs appears much less than 1%
- Multinational study of 2622 patients with SCAs: 61% underwent surgical resection; only 0.1% diagnosed with serous cystadenocarcinoma
- More common problem: local invasion causing early satiety, obstructive jaundice, and pain
- Large lesions more likely symptomatic
- Risk of invasive carcinoma associated with female gender, older age at detection, and larger cyst size >10 cm

## Mucinous Cystic Neoplasms: Definition
- MCNs are mucin-producing cystic tumors
- Lack communication with the pancreatic duct
- Contain mucin-producing columnar epithelium
- Ovarian-like stroma surrounding columnar epithelium is pathognomonic
- Presumed reason MCNs are almost exclusively found in females
- Ovarian stroma shared with mucinous cysts of ovary and liver
- MCNs classified separately from IPMNs by WHO since 1996

## MCN: Clinical and Imaging Features
- Most commonly found in body and tail of pancreas
- Size ranges from small 2 cm to large 25 cm
- Many MCNs discovered incidentally
- Symptoms: abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, back pain, recurrent pancreatitis, rarely jaundice
- Any macrocystic lesion in distal pancreas of a female patient should be highly suspicious for MCN
- Often unilocular but may contain septa
- Multilocular lesions typically macrocystic, in contrast to SCAs which are microcystic
- Peripheral eggshell calcifications best demonstrated on noncontrast CT
- Mural nodularity concerning for invasion
- Gross: round, smooth surface, fibrous pseudocapsule

## MCN: Invasive Risk and Prognosis
- MCNs have risk for harboring invasive carcinoma
- Rates of invasive disease range from 10% to 50%
- May be underestimate because benign and malignant epithelium may coexist
- Extensive pathologic evaluation is critical for accurate diagnosis
- Multicenter US analysis: overall rate of invasive carcinoma in MCN lesions up to 15%
- Factors associated with invasive risk:
  - Male gender
  - Pancreatic head and neck location
  - Larger MCN
  - Mural nodules
  - Duct dilation
- Natural history not well defined due to rarity
- 5-year disease-specific survival for invasive carcinoma: 57% to 64%

## IPMN: Definition and Epidemiology
- IPMNs are epithelial tumors arising from main pancreatic duct or branch ducts
- Cause ductal dilation from mucin production
- Unified diagnosis by WHO in 1996
- Increasing identification of asymptomatic cystic lesions with high-quality cross-sectional imaging
- Significant percentage of incidentally discovered cysts are IPMNs
- IPMNs occur equally in men and women
- More often found in older individuals; peak incidence 50 to 70 years
- IPMNs represent approximately 15% to 30% of cystic neoplasms in large series
- Early reports may have mixed IPMN and MCN; interpret with caution

## IPMN: Radiographic Classification
- IPMN believed to involve entire pancreas
- Radiographically detectable disease may involve main duct alone, branch ducts alone, or both
- Main-duct IPMN: diffuse or segmental dilatation of main pancreatic duct >5 mm without other obstruction
- Branch-duct IPMN: communication with main pancreatic duct without significant main duct dilation
- BD-IPMN may be unilocular, multilocular, with septations or mural nodularity
- Without septations, mural nodules, or solid component, BD-IPMN may be indistinguishable from retention cysts, MCNs, small cystic endocrine tumors, or pseudocysts
- Mixed IPMN: branch-duct dilation associated with main-duct dilation >5 mm

## IPMN: Malignant Risk by Subtype
- Radiographic subtype is one of strongest predictors of high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer
- MD-IPMN:
  - Up to 60% are malignant high-grade dysplasia and invasive cancer
  - Up to 45% have invasive adenocarcinoma
  - Generally, patients with MD-IPMN should undergo resection
- BD-IPMN:
  - Invasive carcinoma or high-grade dysplasia reported in 12% to 30% of resected patients
- Mixed IPMN:
  - Rates of invasive carcinoma or high-grade dysplasia generally between BD-IPMN and MD-IPMN
- This classification forms backbone of IPMN management paradigm

## IPMN: Histologic Subtypes
- Gastric type: papillae often mingled with tubular glands resembling pyloric glands
- Intestinal type: villous papillae; tall columnar cells; pseudostratified cigar-shaped nuclei; basophilic cytoplasm; variable apical mucin
- Pancreatobiliary type: complex branching papillae; columnar cells with marked atypical nuclei; neutral or basophilic cytoplasm
- Oncocytic type: arborizing papillae; cells with enlarged round nuclei; eosinophilic cytoplasm due to abundant mitochondria
- Classification based on histologic appearance, mucin gene expression, and tissue architecture
- Each subtype exhibits a particular risk of invasive carcinoma

## IPMN: Dysplasia Grading
- Revised classification system and Baltimore consensus recommendations
- IPMNs graded as:
  - Low-grade dysplasia
  - High-grade dysplasia
  - Invasive carcinoma
- Multiple degrees of dysplasia can coexist in a resected IPMN specimen
- Pathologists generally report the highest grade of dysplasia in the resected lesion
- Accurate grading is important for prognosis and management

## IPMN-Associated Cancer: Incidence
- Invasive carcinoma arising from IPMN is well documented
- Invasive cancer found in 20% to 50% of resected IPMN specimens
- Japanese series of 1404 patients with BD-IPMN:
  - Overall incidence of invasive carcinoma: 3.3% at 5 years, 6.6% at 10 years, 15.0% at 15 years
- Massachusetts General Hospital study:
  - Rate of high-grade or invasive cancer: 5.5%
  - Invasive cancer developed in 4.4%
- Patients with IPMN are at increased risk for conventional pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma elsewhere in pancreas: 1% to 8%

## IPMN-Associated Cancer: Risk Factors
- Symptoms at presentation:
  - Jaundice
  - Pancreatitis
  - New-onset diabetes
- Larger lesions: cyst size ≥3 cm
- Abrupt change in caliber of pancreatic duct with distal pancreatic atrophy
- Mural nodules
- Main-duct dilation
- Cyst growth over time
- Elevated serum CA19-9 levels

## IPMN-Associated Cancer: Prognosis
- Reported 5-year survival for IPMN-associated invasive cancer: 43% to 60%
- Compared with ductal adenocarcinoma: 15% 5-year survival after resection
- Poultsides et al. Johns Hopkins experience:
  - IPMN-associated cancers had lower rates of advanced T stage and lymph node metastasis
  - Ductal adenocarcinoma more often had high-grade lesions, perineural invasion, vascular invasion, and positive margins
  - If adverse tumor-related factors present, outcome similar to ductal adenocarcinoma
- Improved outcome of IPMN-associated cancer may be due to earlier stage at resection
- Findings confirmed in meta-analysis of 12 comparative studies

## IPMN-Associated Cancer: Variants
- Colloid-subtype invasive IPMN: significantly better survival than conventional pancreatic carcinoma and invasive tubular IPMN
- Tubular-variant and lymph node involvement: negative prognostic factors
- Conventional adenocarcinoma: more often obstructive jaundice, perineural/vascular invasion, regional lymph node metastasis
- Pooled analysis:
  - Tubular adenocarcinoma had poor overall survival HR 1.90 compared with colloid carcinoma
  - Survival similar to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

## Genetics of IPMN
- Shares many molecular alterations with pancreatic cancer:
  - KRAS mutations
  - Loss of p16
  - TP53 mutations
- Key differences:
  - SMAD4/DPC4 inactivated in more than half of pancreatic adenocarcinomas
  - SMAD4/DPC4 preserved in virtually all noninvasive IPMNs
  - Lost in only 10% of colloid cancers arising in intestinal-type IPMN
  - GNAS mutations described in as many as 66% of IPMNs
  - GNAS mutations not found in other pancreatic cystic neoplasms or invasive adenocarcinomas not associated with IPMN
- GNAS mutations predominant in colloid carcinoma; KRAS uncommon
- KRAS mutations much more common in tubular carcinoma; GNAS uncommon
- Concomitant pancreatic adenocarcinoma tends to develop in pancreas with IPMNs with wild-type GNAS, regardless of BD- or MD-IPMN subtype
- Whole-exome sequencing: IPMNs had alterations of RNF43, GNAS, or KRAS; never VHL or CTNNB1
- Molecular genetic analysis combined with clinical and radiologic data improves diagnosis and may predict progression

## Diagnostic Evaluation: Cross-Sectional Imaging
- High-quality cross-sectional imaging is key to diagnostic evaluation
- Multidetector CT allows thin-section imaging of pancreas
- Most common method for evaluation of pancreatic cysts
- Pancreatic protocol CT:
  - Carefully delineates and characterizes pancreatic parenchyma near cystic lesion
  - Critical in assessing for radiographically occult invasive cancer causing adjacent pancreatic duct dilation
  - Allows evaluation of septations, mural nodules, and calcifications
- MRCP:
  - Defines cyst morphology
  - May be better than CT for determining connection with pancreatic duct, enhancing mural nodule, or internal septations
- Secretin-enhanced MRCP improves visualization of connection between pancreatic cyst and main pancreatic duct

## Diagnostic Evaluation: EUS
- EUS is adjunct to other imaging modalities if pancreas cyst has concerning or radiologic features
- Also used to obtain cyst fluid for cytology and biochemical analysis
- Procedure is operator dependent; expertise valuable
- Distinction between mucin clots or debris and mural nodules is clinically important
- Contrast-enhanced EUS:
  - One of most accurate diagnostic modalities for discrimination
  - Characterizes vascularity by detecting signals from microbubbles in vessels after IV contrast

## Diagnostic Evaluation: Confocal Laser Endomicroscopy
- New promising technique to differentiate pancreatic cyst types
- Shows real-time visualization of pancreatic cyst with microscopic detail
- Endoscopic probe introduced through a 19-gauge needle
- Each pancreatic cyst type has specific imaging pattern:
  - SCA: superficial vascular network or fern pattern is highly specific
  - MCN: single or multiple layers of epithelium without papillary configuration, called epithelial bands
  - IPMN: finger-like papillae is characteristic

## Cyst Fluid Analysis
- EUS-fine-needle aspiration is low-risk; complication rate 2% to 3%
- Markers evaluated: CA19-9, CEA, CA15-3, mucin proteins, KRAS, amylase
- Brugge et al.: cyst fluid CEA >192 ng/mL best predictor of mucinous lesion
- Accurately defined mucinous lesions in 79% of cases
- Cyst fluid CEA elevation plus extracellular mucin: positive predictive value up to 85%
- SCAs and pancreatic retention cysts uniformly have undetectable CEA
- CEA measurement does not predict presence of invasive disease
- Cyst fluid glucose: potential biomarker for mucinous pancreatic cyst
  - Similar diagnostic accuracy to standard CEA, amylase, and cytology
  - Improved efficiency
- Cyst fluid amylase:
  - Low amylase useful to exclude pseudocyst
  - High amylase not helpful; may be found in SCAs, IPMNs, and MCNs
- Cytology limitations: small volume, low cellular content, contamination with mucin and mucin-producing cells from stomach or duodenum
- Through-the-needle forceps device: investigational approach for EUS-guided tissue acquisition

## Molecular Markers and CompCyst
- Molecular events leading to cyst formation: KRAS mutation, p53 mutation, loss of p16 and SMAD4
- Mutations or deletions in SMAD4, CDKN2A, TP53, PIK3CA and/or PTEN associated with advanced neoplasia
- KRAS mutation followed by allelic loss initially felt strongly predictive of malignant cyst
- Validation studies mixed:
  - KRAS mutation alone: high specificity but very low sensitivity at 11%
  - Molecular analysis alone lower sensitivity 76.5% vs CEA measurement alone detecting 82.4% of mucinous lesions
- Novel murine monoclonal antibody Das-1: high sensitivity and specificity for high-risk and invasive carcinoma
- CompCyst machine-learning method:
  - Integrates clinical symptoms, imaging, and genetic mutations from cyst fluid
  - Mutations include KRAS, GNAS, RNF43, CDKN2A, CTNNB1, TP53, BRAF, VHL, PIK3CA
  - Diagnoses and determines likely best course of action
  - More accurate than management dictated by conventional clinical and imaging criteria alone
  - Potential to reduce patient morbidity and economic costs

## Box 60.1: Indications for EUS Evaluation
- European 2018:
  - If EUS changes clinical management
  - Cyst clinical or radiologic features of concern identified during initial investigation or surveillance
- IAP 2017:
  - Growth rate ≥5 mm over 2 years
  - Increased levels of serum CA19-9
  - MPD dilatation between 5 and 9 mm
  - Cyst diameter ≥3 cm
  - Acute pancreatitis caused by IPMN
  - Enhancing mural nodule <5 mm
  - Abrupt change in caliber of MPD with distal pancreatic atrophy
  - Lymphadenopathy
  - Thickened/enhancing cyst walls

## Treatment Principles
- If histopathology of cystic neoplasm can be diagnosed by clinical and imaging criteria:
  - Treatment recommendations should be based on known behavior of that specific histologic entity
- In some instances, most often small cysts:
  - Exact histopathologic diagnosis cannot be determined without formal pancreatectomy
- Under these circumstances:
  - Treatment recommendations based on radiographic and inferred histopathology after comprehensive diagnostic evaluation

## Treatment: Serous Cystadenoma
- When radiographic and/or endoscopic findings characteristic of SCA:
  - Resection reserved for young patients with significant growth
  - Clearly symptomatic lesions
  - Prevention of complications related to occlusion of splenic and/or portal veins
- Asymptomatic patients: risk of invasive carcinoma less than 1%
- Risk associated with pancreatectomy much greater than risk of cancer
- Tseng et al.:
  - Radiographically followed 24 patients with SCA for median 23 months
  - Median growth rate 0.6 cm per year
  - Larger lesions ≥4 cm had higher growth rate 1.98 cm/year vs <4 cm 0.12 cm/year
  - Recommended all SCAs larger than 4 cm should be resected regardless of symptoms
- Memorial Sloan Kettering study: no association between larger size and faster growth
- Multicenter study of 2622 patients with SCA:
  - Risk of invasive carcinoma estimated very low
  - Surgical treatment recommended only to minority with uncertain diagnosis, significant related symptoms, or exceptional concern for invasive carcinoma
- Management should mainly follow conservative approach:
  - Follow asymptomatic patients
  - Monitor progression in size and appearance or onset of symptoms
- Surgical resection considered only for:
  - Symptomatic patients
  - Potentially malignant tumor
  - Diagnostic dilemma
- Large SCAs: decisions case-by-case considering age, tumor location, comorbidities
- Young patient without comorbidity with potentially growing body/tail lesion: candidate for function-preserving minimally invasive surgical resection
- Otherwise, large SCAs can be strictly followed; resection considered only for symptoms or rapid increase in cyst size

## Treatment: Mucinous Cystic Neoplasms
- 2012 International Association of Pancreatology guidelines: resection for all MCNs regardless of size
- European guidelines 2018: resection for MCNs with:
  - Cyst dimension 4 cm or larger
  - Enhancing mural nodules
  - Symptoms related to cyst: jaundice, acute pancreatitis, new-onset diabetes
- European 2018: MCN less than 4 cm and otherwise asymptomatic can be safely followed every 6 months for 1 year, then yearly
- Multiple studies: small indeterminate MCNs without symptoms or high-risk features can safely be observed
- MCNs more often located in distal pancreas
- May be amenable to splenic preservation and laparoscopic resection, demonstrated safe and feasible
- Systematic review of 13 studies with 773 patients:
  - No risk of progression after resection of MCN without invasive cancer
  - Resected MCN with low-grade or high-grade dysplasia do not require surveillance
- This is an additional argument for resection, particularly in young patients
- Unlike IPMN, MCN does not require long-term lifelong follow-up
- Features concerning for invasive carcinoma: formal pancreatectomy
- If patient has mucinous cystadenocarcinoma: postoperative surveillance as for pancreatic cancer

## Treatment: MD-IPMN and Mixed-Type IPMN
- When MD-IPMN identified on cross-sectional imaging, operative resection generally recommended
- These lesions have high risk of harboring high-grade dysplasia or invasive disease
- Even when invasive carcinoma or high-grade dysplasia does not exist at presentation, most if not all MD-IPMNs will progress to invasive carcinoma
- Careful assessment of local resectability should be performed before operative intervention
- Historically, mixed-type IPMNs treated like MD-IPMN
- MGH group: minimal involvement of main pancreatic duct does not carry same malignant potential as true MD-IPMN
- International consensus for main-duct/mixed-type IPMN with pancreatic duct dilation ≥5 mm:
  - 41% of experts advised nonoperative surveillance every 3 to 6 months
  - 59% advised operative intervention
- European 2018 guidelines:
  - Main pancreatic duct dilation 10 mm or greater: absolute indication for surgical resection
  - 5 to 9 mm: relative indication
- IAP 2017:
  - Surgical resection for all MD-IPMNs with main pancreatic duct at least 10 mm
  - Main pancreatic duct 5 to 9 mm considered worrisome features
  - No recommendation for immediate surgical resection; EUS evaluation recommended

## MD-IPMN: Extent of Resection
- Goal of surgery in MD-IPMN: resection of invasive carcinoma and high-grade dysplasia
- If possible, removal of all high-risk disease
- When presence of invasive cancer ascertained preoperatively:
  - Standard resection with lymphadenectomy should be considered
- Prognosis of patients with invasive IPMN dominated by biology and outcome of invasive component
- Development of additional invasive or noninvasive disease in remnant MD-IPMN is of less concern
- Total pancreatectomy generally avoided when preoperative testing suggests invasive cancer in setting of IPMN
- MD-IPMN limited to part of pancreas and no overt radiologic evidence of invasive cancer:
  - Resect IPMN-containing pancreas
  - Head: pancreatoduodenectomy
  - Body and tail: distal pancreatectomy
- Partial pancreatectomy for IPMN:
  - Intraoperative frozen-section evaluation focused on identification of high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer at margin
- Positive margin for high-grade dysplasia:
  - Should be resected
  - High-risk disease at margin is significant predictor of future remnant progression
- 2017 IAP guidelines:
  - Low-grade dysplasia at margin: no further resection required
  - Risk of progression to cancer minimal
  - High-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma at margin: prompt additional resection
  - Some advocate total pancreatectomy if negative margin cannot be achieved
- Frozen section cannot capture discontinuous skipped lesions of main pancreatic duct

## MD-IPMN: Diffuse Involvement and Total Pancreatectomy
- Patients with MD-IPMN diffusely involving whole gland pose difficult management dilemma
- Ductal dilation throughout pancreas could be due to:
  - MD-IPMN extending throughout pancreatic duct
  - Outflow obstruction caused by invasive carcinoma or IPMN in head
  - Dilation may occur proximal or distal to high-risk lesion due to overproduction of mucin
- Without clear signs of invasive carcinoma such as mass effect, intraductal mass, or nodules:
  - Ductal dilation does not help localize invasive cancer
- IPMN considered a field defect within entire ductal system
- Concern: resection of just part of pancreas leaves patient with remnant pancreas with significant risk for developing pancreatic adenocarcinoma
- Greater concern in young patients because remnant pancreas has longer time for development of invasive carcinoma
- Must balance morbidity, mortality, and quality of life of total pancreatectomy
- Study of 329 patients undergoing total pancreatectomy at two high-volume centers 2000-2014:
  - Operative morbidity 59.3%
  - 30-day operative mortality 2.1%
  - QoL assessed with SF-36, EORTC QLQ-PAN26, Diabetes Dependent questionnaires
  - Young age, abdominal pain, worse body image negatively associated with physical component of SF-36
  - Diabetes, sexual satisfaction, perception of body image affected mental component of SF-36
- Another study of 93 patients total pancreatectomy French multicentric 2004-2013:
  - Postoperative mortality 4.3%
  - Morbidity 47.3%
- Total pancreatectomy is a viable option for patients with main-duct IPMN with diffuse involvement and high risk for developing invasive carcinoma

## Postoperative Surveillance After Pancreatectomy for IPMN
- When less than total pancreatectomy is performed, postoperative surveillance warranted in all patients
- Noninvasive IPMN: follow for development of additional lesions in remnant gland
- Invasive disease: follow for distant recurrence and gland recurrence
- No consensus on best follow-up strategy
- IAP 2017 guidelines:
  - Follow-up at least twice a year in patients with:
    - Family history of pancreatic cancer
    - Surgical resection margin with high-grade dysplasia
    - Resected IPMN of nonintestinal subtype
  - Follow-up every 6 to 12 months in all other patients with resected IPMNs
- European 2018 guidelines:
  - Follow-up every 6 months for first 2 years, then yearly
  - For IPMNs with high-grade dysplasia or main duct involvement after pancreatectomy
  - IPMN with low-grade dysplasia followed same way as nonresected IPMN
- Completion pancreatectomy indicated for treatment of detected progression thought to be high-grade dysplasia or invasive disease

## Treatment: BD-IPMN Resection Indications
- Resection reserved for selected patients with BD-IPMN
- 2017 IAP guidelines classify concerning radiographic features into worrisome features and high-risk stigmata
- High-risk stigmata: patients should undergo resection without further testing
  - Obstructive jaundice in patient with cystic lesion of pancreatic head
  - Enhancing mural nodule ≥5 mm
  - Main pancreatic duct ≥10 mm
- Worrisome features: patients should undergo further evaluation with EUS
  - Pancreatitis
  - Cyst ≥3 cm
  - Enhancing mural nodule <5 mm
  - Thickened/enhancing cyst walls
  - Main duct size 5 to 9 mm
  - Abrupt change in caliber of pancreatic duct with distal pancreatic atrophy
  - Lymphadenopathy
  - Increased serum level of CA19-9
  - Cyst growth rate >5 mm over 2 years
- EUS also recommended for cysts greater than 3 cm without worrisome features to verify absence of thickened walls or mural nodules
- Multicentric study of nonoperative patients with presumed IPMNs:
  - Worrisome features: 5-year disease-specific survival 96%; conservative management appropriate
  - High-risk stigma: 40% risk of IPMN-related death; surgical resection policy

## BD-IPMN: European 2018 Guidelines
- Similar recommendations to 2017 IAP for resection of BD-IPMN
- Absolute indications for surgery:
  - Jaundice
  - Cytology positive for high-grade dysplasia or cancer
  - Presence of contrast-enhancing mural nodule ≥5 mm
  - Solid mass
- Relative indications for surgery:
  - Growth rate ≥5 mm/year
  - Increased serum CA19.9 >37 U/mL in absence of jaundice
  - Main pancreatic duct diameter between 5 and 9.9 mm
  - Cyst size ≥4 cm
  - New-onset diabetes mellitus or acute pancreatitis
  - Contrast-enhancing mural nodules <5 mm
- Patients with relative indications: closer follow-up or resection based on comorbidities

## Surgical Approaches for BD-IPMN
- Branch-duct lesions in head of pancreas: pancreatoduodenectomy
- Branch-duct lesions in tail: distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy
- Recently, pancreas-sparing procedures reported to maintain exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function:
  - Enucleation
  - Central pancreatectomy
  - Resection of uncinate process
- Single institutional study:
  - Pancreas-sparing pancreatectomy attempted in 91 patients
  - Feasible in 81 patients 89%
  - Enucleation most common pancreas-sparing procedure
- Acceptable mortality
- Higher-than-expected morbidity compared with standard pancreatic resections, mainly pancreatic fistula
- Whether pancreas-sparing pancreatectomy preserves pancreatic exocrine and endocrine function requires further investigation

## Solid Pseudopapillary Tumor: Epidemiology
- SPTs also known as Frantz or Hamoudi tumors
- Named after pathologists who first described entity in 1950s
- Rare tumors; account for as many as 2.5% of resected pancreatic neoplasms
- Predominately in young women
- Often discovered when patients experience symptoms
- Review of 2744 patients from English literature:
  - Female to male ratio 9:1
  - Mean age 29 years
  - Only 38% asymptomatic at presentation
  - 64% had pain
  - 33% had a mass
  - Mean tumor size 8.6 cm
  - Most common location: tail and body pancreas 59.3%
- May present acutely with rupture of capsule and hemoperitoneum, but uncommon
- Review of 292 reported cases found 8 cases with acute rupture

## SPT: Imaging and Pathology
- Cross-sectional imaging: encapsulated lesions with irregular areas of hypodensity secondary to necrosis or hemorrhage
- Wall may reveal calcifications
- Cystic degeneration makes differentiation from pseudocyst or other pancreatic cystic neoplasms difficult
- Young female with well-encapsulated pancreatic mass with cystic and solid components: SPT should be top differential diagnosis
- Differentiating features: combination of solid and cystic components with gradual degenerative changes resulting in pseudopapillae formation
- SPTs distinct from normal pancreatic parenchyma; rarely cause ductal dilation due to lack of invasion
- MRI: areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images correspond to hemorrhagic necrosis or hemorrhagic debris
- Gross: tan or yellow, well circumscribed, smooth on palpation
- Opened: irregular cystic cavities with areas of necrosis or hemorrhage
- Histology: polygonal epithelial cells arranged in discohesive pattern
- Boundaries resemble mass effect as opposed to being invasive
- Immunohistochemical staining: vimentin, keratin, neuron-specific enolase, CD10, progesterone common
- Rarely express chromogranin or estrogen
- Abnormal β-catenin expression present; KRAS, p53, and DPC4 appear unaltered
- Aggressive phenotypes: high mitotic rate, nuclear atypia, spindling of tumor cells, anaplastic giant tumor cells consistent with sarcomatoid carcinoma
- Molecular alterations: Wnt/β-catenin, Hedgehog, androgen receptor signaling pathways, and epithelial mesenchymal transition genes activated
- Role of genetic testing in diagnosis of SPTs not extensively investigated

## SPT: Management and Prognosis
- Clinically generally indolent
- Typically cured with complete surgical extirpation
- Many series demonstrate long-term survival after resection
- Significant vascular invasion: most common reason for inability to resect
- Metastatic disease present in as many as 15%
- Criteria for defining SPTs as malignant:
  - Locally advanced disease with vascular invasion precluding resection
  - Lymph node or hepatic metastasis
- Long-term survival often possible despite malignant factors such as metastatic disease
- Should not preclude resection in selected cases
- Meta-analysis 2002-2017:
  - Progression rate after initial surgery in patients with nonmetastatic SPTs ~2.6%
  - Male gender, positive lymph nodes, positive margin at resection, and lymphovascular invasion associated with risk of progression

## Other Cystic Pancreatic Neoplasms
- Benign cystic lesions include lymphoepithelial cysts, simple cysts, and mucinous nonneoplastic cysts
- Pseudocysts are nonneoplastic, devoid of epithelial lining
- Pseudocyst management includes observation, endoscopic drainage, or operative drainage
- Cystic neoplasms are heterogeneous
- Most common encountered by surgeons: IPMNs, MCNs, SCAs
- Multidisciplinary evaluation is essential

## Conclusions
- Diagnosis of cystic lesions of the pancreas is increasing
- Most common lesions: IPMNs, MCNs, and SCAs
- Despite multiple clinical guidelines, no definitive strategy to differentiate between various cyst types
- Patients with pancreas cysts should be discussed by multidisciplinary team in centers with expertise in diagnosis and surgical treatment
- SCAs should be considered benign; asymptomatic patients can be followed radiographically
- Most patients with mucinous lesions should undergo resection, especially with concerning features:
  - Size greater than 3 cm
  - Solid component
  - Ductal dilation
- Initial evaluation of small, benign-appearing cyst should include one early interval image to ensure no occult invasive carcinoma or high-grade dysplasia causing retention cyst
- More clinicians adopting selective approach
- Improvements in determining histopathologic subtypes without resection
- High-quality cross-sectional imaging and EUS with cyst fluid analysis help subtype many pancreatic cystic neoplasms
- Advancements in biomarkers from cyst fluid should lead to better identification of mucinous subtypes and obviate need for resection in some patients

## Key Takeaways
- Cystic neoplasms include IPMN, MCN, SCA, and SPT; pseudocysts are nonneoplastic
- MD-IPMN has high malignant risk; BD-IPMN resection is selective based on worrisome features and high-risk stigmata
- MCN has 10%-50% invasive risk; ovarian-type stroma; almost exclusively female
- SCA is generally benign; resect for symptoms, significant growth, or diagnostic uncertainty
- SPT occurs in young women; complete surgical extirpation is usually curative
- Cyst fluid CEA >192 ng/mL predicts mucinous cyst; molecular markers and CompCyst are evolving
- Surveillance after resection depends on dysplasia grade, IPMN subtype, and extent of resection
